name: Joel

facts.author: Joel the son of Pethuel (1:1). Nothing more is known of him, but he seems to have lived in Judah and to have known the temple well.
facts.audience: The people, elders and priests of Judah and Jerusalem

about: Joel was written after a terrible plague of locusts. Swarm after swarm had eaten the crops, the vines and the fig trees (1:4), and drought had followed. The grain offerings at the temple had stopped, and the people were in despair.

Joel saw in this disaster a warning of the day of the LORD, a day of judgement still greater. He called the people to turn to God with all their heart, with fasting and weeping, for the LORD is gracious and merciful (2:12-13). Then the LORD promises to pity His people, to drive the invader away and to restore the years the locusts had eaten.

More than that, God promises to pour out His Spirit on all people, young and old, men and women (2:28-29), and everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved (2:32). The apostle Peter preached from these words on the day of Pentecost. The book ends with the judgement of the nations and a picture of the LORD dwelling in Zion.

themes.title: The day of the LORD
themes.text: The locust plague points to a greater day when God will judge all the nations.

themes.title: True repentance
themes.text: God wants hearts that are torn in sorrow for sin, not only torn clothes (2:13).

themes.title: The Spirit poured out
themes.text: God promises His Spirit to all His people, not only to a few prophets and kings.

themes.title: Restoration
themes.text: The LORD will give back what was lost and will live among His people in Zion.
